items.summary:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports leafnode connections between servers and message tracing through NATS headers.

### Problem Description

Message trace destination checks were applied to ordinary client connections but not consistently to messages arriving through leafnode connections.

A leafnode operator could cause trace events to be sent to subjects that would not otherwise be permitted and could use trace-only behavior to prevent normal delivery or storage of affected messages.

Trace events can include routing, subscription, account, service import and JetStream metadata. The payload of the original application message is not chosen through the trace event itself.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.7 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.8.

### Workarounds

Where possible, avoid granting publish paths from less-trusted leaf nodes into subjects for which trace-only behavior would affect delivery guarantees. No other known workarounds are available aside from upgrading to a fixed release.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-p3j5-5hrq-p75h>
 * Credit: Koda Reef

items.summary:
## Summary

Route selection uses the raw un-normalized request path, and the per-route ACL and basic-auth gates hang off that selection, so a dot-segment, encoded-dot, or double-slash variant of a protected path selects a different route, skips both gates, and is forwarded to the backend which normalizes and serves the protected resource. Unauthenticated; complete bypass of the access control the operator configured. Confirmed at HEAD b841544. Direct peers: Traefik CVE-2023-47106, Envoy CVE-2019-9901.

## The defect

fabio never normalizes the request path. A repository-wide search for path.Clean returns zero results. Route selection uses the raw path (route/table.go line 487: `if target = t.lookup(h, req.URL.Path, pick, match); target != nil {`). Both access-control gates are properties of the target that lookup returned:

```go
// proxy/http_proxy.go
if t.AccessDeniedHTTP(r) {                      // line 111, per-route allow / deny:ip ACL
    http.Error(w, "access denied", http.StatusForbidden)
    return
}
if !t.Authorized(r, w, p.AuthSchemes) {          // line 116, per-route auth= basic auth
    http.Error(w, "authorization failed", http.StatusUnauthorized)
    return
}
```

and the same raw path is forwarded verbatim (`Path: r.URL.Path` at line 142). So /./admin/, /%2e/admin/, //admin/ and /x/../admin/ do not match the protected /admin route. They fall through to the catch-all / route, which carries no ACL and no auth, and fabio forwards the un-normalized path to the origin, which normalizes it and serves the protected resource.

## Verification

Verified end to end against the real binary at HEAD, not a synthetic unit test. fabio was built and run with static routes against a `python3 -m http.server` origin, driven with curl --path-as-is: on a basic-auth route, /admin/ returned 401 without credentials and 200 with valid credentials (controls correct), while all four crafted paths returned 200 with the protected page and NO credentials; on an ACL route, /admin/ returned 403 and all four crafted variants returned 200.

Precondition, stated honestly: a less restrictive route must reach the same backend so the crafted path has somewhere to fall through to. That is exactly the two-tag urlprefix- shape fabio's own access-control documentation instructs operators to configure. Where no fallback route exists the request 404s instead.

## Suggested fix

Normalize the path before route lookup: decode percent-encoded dot segments and apply path.Clean, then match. Whether the normalized or original path is forwarded upstream is a separate decision, but the LOOKUP must run on the normalized form, because the ACL and auth decisions are derived from it. Also lowercase and strip the port and any trailing dot from the request host before host matching. Secondary observations: X-Forwarded-Prefix is passed through from the client on non-strip routes; the gRPC proxy path never calls either authorization gate, so allow=/auth= on a proto=grpc route are silently unenforced.

## Dedup note

The obvious residual of CVE-2025-48865 is already taken: CVE-2026-62987 / GHSA-fq95-v8xc-jm3v (published 2026-07-03) covers the Connection-header strip of proxy.header.clientip/tls/requestid, fixed in v1.7.2. Do not re-report that. The finding above is a different and independent defect.

## Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The bypass was reproduced against the real fabio binary with a live backend, including the 401-vs-200 and 403-vs-200 controls, and the reporter separately confirmed at HEAD that lookup takes req.URL.Path, that both gates derive from the returned target, that the raw path is forwarded, and that path.Clean appears nowhere in the repository.

The reporter manually verified this finding against the project's source at the location cited above before reporting it; the AI assistance noted above was for the audit and the drafting.

### Summary
A remote Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability, allows any remote client to cause a complete crash of the Aedes MQTT broker process. This is achieved by sending a specially crafted MQTT message (via PUBLISH or SUBSCRIBE), or by setting a Will message with such a topic, containing a highly recursive topic string (e.g., with thousands of '/' delimiters). The lack of input validation and error handling leads to an uncaught exception in an internal routing library, terminating the entire Node.js application.

### Details
The Aedes broker fails to enforce limits on the depth or structural complexity of MQTT topic strings. When a client publishes to or subscribes to a topic with excessive levels of recursion, the internal routing logic cascading into the qlobber library (via mqemitter) reaches an hard-coded limit within the qlobber._split_words function.

This function throws a hard Error: too many words (found in lib/qlobber.js:604). Crucially, Aedes does not wrap the calls to these internal modules (such as in handlers/subscribe.js or the publishing logic) in try-catch blocks. Consequently, this exception propagates up to the main Node.js event loop as an unhandled exception, causing the entire broker process to crash immediately.

This vulnerability affects all stable versions of Aedes due to the underlying dependency behavior and missing perimetral validation.

Stack Trace from Crash:
```Plaintext

aedes-broker  | 	throw new Error('too many words');
aedes-broker  | 	^
aedes-broker  | 
aedes-broker  | Error: too many words
aedes-broker  |     at Qlobber._split_words (/app/node_modules/mqemitter/node_modules/qlobber/lib/qlobber.js:604:15)
aedes-broker  |     at Qlobber._split (/app/node_modules/mqemitter/node_modules/qlobber/lib/qlobber.js:624:18)
aedes-broker  |     at Qlobber.add (/app/node_modules/mqemitter/node_modules/qlobber/lib/qlobber.js:651:43)
aedes-broker  |     at MQEmitter.on (/app/node_modules/mqemitter/mqemitter.js:65:17)

aedes-broker  |     at SubState.addSubs (/app/node_modules/aedes/lib/handlers/subscribe.js:167:12)
```

items.summary: Traefik is a HTTP reverse proxy and load balancer. In versions >= v3.7.0 and <= v3.7.11, the Kubernetes ingress-nginx provider mishandles Ingresses that carry both an authentication annotation and the nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/from-to-www-redirect annotation. For such Ingresses the provider creates an additional 'sibling' router that matches on the host alone, carries only the RedirectRegex middleware, and still points at the parent router's protected backend service. Because RedirectRegex is not a terminal handler, a request its pattern does not match is forwarded to the backend, and because the redirect pattern only accepts a numeric port while Traefik's host matcher canonicalizes the authority via net.SplitHostPort, a request with a non-numeric or empty port (for example 'Host: www.example.com:x') selects the sibling router, misses the redirect, and is proxied to the protected backend with none of the Ingress's annotation-derived middlewares applied. This discards not only authentication (e.g. BasicAuth) but every annotation-derived middleware, including source-IP allowlisting. Traefik v2 and v3 releases before v3.7.0 are not affected. The issue is fixed in v3.7.12.

CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.
items.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions

This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.

items.summary: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.

items.summary: High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain. We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent represents vulnerabilities and functional gadgets--intended program behaviors that can be repurposed in attacks--through preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection. It searches backward from unmet preconditions for capability producers and forward from discovered capabilities for functional gadgets that consume or amplify them. Object-centered chaining knowledge from our empirical study directs searches toward promising vulnerability classes, functional operations, and object accesses. We evaluate ChainAgent against Codex, a general-purpose coding agent, on 15 PHP applications across three shared LLM backends. ChainAgent achieves 42.02%--44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct goal-reaching dependency edges as Codex. An additional evaluation of 30 real-world PHP applications identifies 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine of which achieve remote code execution (RCE).
items.title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery in PHP Web Applications

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in investment research, and many studies report promising historical returns. However, such results are only credible if researchers can demonstrate that the model used only information available at the time, account for how strategies and configurations were selected, and explain how reported returns were generated. We identify six common threats to validity in LLM investment evaluations and apply them to 18 published studies. Across 108 assessments, we find substantial gaps in reporting. No paper fully addresses information timing, model-memory exposure, universe selection, trading costs, or configuration-selection bias. Only four studies provide minimum evidence that results hold across multiple market periods. Our analysis reveals that commonly used safeguards often address different problems than researchers assume. For example, using dated inputs does not guarantee that a pretrained model lacked knowledge of future events, and repeated experimental runs do not correct for strategy-selection bias. We therefore propose an evaluation protocol for future LLM investment research. Rather than judging whether LLMs can generate profits, our study examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to support such claims. We conclude that current reporting practices are generally insufficient for that purpose.
items.title: Evaluating LIM Trading Agents: A Critical Review of Backtesting Validity and Reporting Practices

items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable high-capacity large language models (LLMs) with high sparse computation, making them attractive for deployment on private hardware. However, distributing model weights exposes valuable intellectual property (IP) to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, creating an urgent need to both verify model ownership and trace leaked copies to individual licensees. Existing model-watermarking techniques are ill-suited for meeting this need because they are fragile under MoE's dynamic routing or require costly retraining to embed a distinct watermark for each licensee, thus making scalable distribution difficult. To address these challenges, we present PPMoE, the first plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for MoE LLMs. Rather than training a separate model per user, PPMoE trains a compact set of mergeable incremental weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, mutually compatible routing patterns. During model distribution, the model owner selectively merges unique combinations of these pre-trained, mutually compatible modules into the base model on the fly, embedding a licensee-specific watermark without additional training. PPMoE supports reliable multi-licensee attribution under both white- and black-box threat models. In the white-box setting, attribution is done by inspecting triggered routing decisions or the merged weight modules responsible for these decisions, whereas in the black-box setting, attribution relies on analyzing output token likelihood ratios. Extensive experiments across five state-of-the-art MoE models, seven benchmark datasets, and varying number of licensees show that PPMoE achieves very high attribution accuracy while preserving base model utility and maintaining strong robustness to various adaptive watermark-removal attacks.
items.title: Plug-and-Play Multi-Licensee Robust Watermarking for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs

A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.

This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies. Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.
Note: Cisco Expressway Series refers to Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) devices and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) devices.

items.summary:
Commit `2b83a60f7763` (5.7.3) hardened the template editor: it added `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` + `CheckTemplateEditorSaveListener` so a non-admin cannot self-grant the `tpl_editor` backend module (editable PHP-capable templates permit server-side code execution). That voter supports only the `modules` field and the literal value `tpl_editor`.

The equally RCE-capable `theme_import` capability lives in a different field - the `themes` checkbox field (tl_user_group.php:98-105 options include `theme_import`; identical on tl_user.php:248-253) - which has no save_callback and no voter. `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` is the only DC voter registered for tl_user_group, and it does not cover the `themes` field. So a delegated user manager can add `theme_import` to their own (or a managed) account.

Live repro (Contao 5.7.9):
1. As admin, create a non-admin backend group with the `user` (or `group`) module (a delegated user manager), and a user in it. Confirm the user cannot access `tpl_editor` (blocked by the 5.7.3 voter).
2. As that non-admin, edit a group/account: add `themes` to the modules field and `theme_import` to the themes field (both accepted - only `tpl_editor` is blocked). Re-authenticate.

## Impact

A delegated user/group manager (a role explicitly not trusted with template/code access) escalates to arbitrary PHP execution on the server, fully compromising the installation. This bypasses the exact protection the 5.7.3 `tpl_editor` fix introduced.

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

items.summary:
### Impact

When fetching objects from a malicious repository, Git LFS may execute an arbitrary command or binary after failing to sufficiently restrict the set of configuration options defined in an `.lfsconfig` file in the repository.

Git LFS permits a limited set of configuration options to be defined in an `.lfsconfig` file at the root of a Git repository, but does not filter these options correctly if their keys contain certain additional components, which allows an attacker to mimic options that configure Git LFS to use a custom command to transfer objects.  An attacker can then provide an arbitrary command which Git LFS will invoke when fetching objects.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by correctly restricting the configuration of custom object transfer commands to local Git configuration files.

### Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 1.3.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

### Workarounds

No single workaround exists other than to disable Git LFS entirely. As far as possible, users and administrators should avoid cloning repositories from untrusted sources.

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:
* For general questions, start a discussion in the Git LFS [discussion forum](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/discussions).
* For reports of additional vulnerabilities, please follow the Git LFS [security reporting policy](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

items.summary:
### Impact

After receiving an HTTP redirection, Git LFS may forward certain HTTP headers to a host other than the one for which they were intended.  While `Authorization` headers are never forwarded to inappropriate hosts, `Cookie` headers may be forwarded incorrectly.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by never forwarding `Cookie` headers to hosts other than the ones for which they were intended.  In particular, after an HTTP redirection is received to a URL with a different scheme, host, or port than found in the URL of the current request, any `Authorization` and `Cookie` headers from the current request will not be sent in the redirected request.

### Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 0.5.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

### Workarounds

No single workaround exists.  As far as possible, users and administrators should review their systems to confirm no unnecessary HTTP redirections are performed, and that HTTP headers other than `Authorization` do not contain privileged or confidential information.

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:
* For general questions, start a discussion in the Git LFS [discussion forum](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/discussions).
* For reports of additional vulnerabilities, please follow the Git LFS [security reporting policy](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

items.summary:
### Impact

When Git LFS makes object transfer or authentication requests to a remote host via SSH, it passes the path component of the remote's SSH URL as part of a command to be executed, but does not properly format the URL's path component as a single argument.  By inserting shell meta-characters into the SSH URL, an attacker may be able to execute arbitrary commands on the remote host, if the host passes the commands to a shell without sanitizing them first.

Git LFS has resolved this problem by fully quoting the arguments of the remote commands it sends via SSH.

As well, Git LFS has resolved a problem with the default HTTPS URLs used when an SSH URL is configured for a remote host and the host either does not support Git LFS remote commands sent via SSH or supports HTTP authentication via SSH for Git LFS but does not return an explicit HTTP URL in response to a `git-lfs-authenticate` remote command.  In these cases, Git LFS now correctly encodes the HTTPS URL used to contact the remote host.

### Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 0.5.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

### Workarounds

Users may set the `lfs.sshTransfer` Git configuration option to `never`, after which Git LFS will not attempt any object transfers over SSH.  However, Git LFS will still make authentication requests to SSH URLs, so administrators of Git LFS services should ensure their systems sanitize all commands received over SSH before executing them.

items.summary:
The IPv6 neighbour discovery code in subsys/net/ip/ipv6_nbr.c keeps packets that are waiting for address resolution on a per-neighbour pending queue. A queued packet holds two references: the one handed over by the sender and a second one taken by net_ipv6_send_ns() when the packet is put on the queue. The Router Advertisement handler handle_ra_input() popped each packet off the queue and passed it to net_send_data(), relying on a trailing nbr_clear_ns_pending() call to release the queue reference — but that call then found the queue already empty and released nothing, so one reference was leaked for every pending packet flushed on an RA.

Router Advertisements are unauthenticated link-local ICMPv6 messages, so any node on the same link can trigger the flush. An attacker can make the leak deterministic by advertising itself as a router without a source link-layer address option, so the victim's neighbour entry stays INCOMPLETE, then inducing the victim to transmit through that next hop (the packet is queued and a neighbour solicitation is sent), leaving the solicitation unanswered and sending a further RA to drain the queue. Each round leaks one struct net_pkt together with its net_buf chain.

Leaked packets are never returned to the fixed-size pools, so the loss is permanent for the lifetime of the boot. With CONFIG_NET_PKT_TX_COUNT defaulting to 4 (14 with CONFIG_NET_PKT_LARGE_DEFAULTS), a small number of repetitions exhausts the transmit packet slab and the node stops being able to send any traffic. The impact is availability only: the reference count is always too high, never too low, so no use-after-free or memory corruption arises.

The fix moves the flush into a helper, nbr_send_pending(), which releases the queue reference for every packet it takes off the queue before handing the remaining reference to net_send_data(), and releases that one too if the send is refused.

items.summary:
The SMSC911x/LAN9220 Ethernet driver stages every outgoing frame in a fixed-size static buffer before pushing it to the controller FIFO. eth_tx() in drivers/ethernet/eth_smsc911x.c took the frame length from net_pkt_get_len(pkt) and passed it directly to net_pkt_read(pkt, tx_buf, total_len), with no comparison against the size of tx_buf (NET_ETH_MAX_FRAME_SIZE). net_pkt_read() takes no destination size and only fails when the packet is shorter than the requested length, so any packet longer than the staging buffer was copied past its end.

Nothing between the IP layer and the driver bounds the frame to what the link can carry: ethernet_send() in subsys/net/l2/ethernet/ethernet.c performs no length check, and the IPv6 output path only compares the packet against the interface MTU when CONFIG_NET_IPV6_FRAGMENT is enabled (it is disabled by default). The size the stack will build is therefore governed by the interface MTU, and that MTU is remotely settable: handle_ra_input() in subsys/net/ip/ipv6_nbr.c honours the MTU option of any Router Advertisement with a value up to 0xffff, gated only by the standard hop-limit-255 and link-local-source checks. An unauthenticated attacker on the same link can raise the MTU and then have the device emit a single frame of several kilobytes, for example as a TCP segment from any service that returns more than ~1.5 KB or as an oversized UDP datagram.

The result is an out-of-bounds write into .bss immediately after tx_buf, with the overrun length and much of its content derived from the transmitted frame. Consequences range from corruption of adjacent kernel data and a crash to potential control-flow influence where the clobbered globals hold pointers; the practical overrun size is bounded by the network buffer pool rather than by the advertised MTU. The fix rejects frames larger than NET_ETH_MAX_FRAME_SIZE with -EMSGSIZE before any TX_DATA_PORT write, so the controller FIFO is also not left holding a command word without its payload.

items.summary:
net_if_ipv4_addr_rm() and net_if_ipv6_addr_rm() in subsys/net/ip/net_if.c unconditionally called net_if_addr_unref() on the target address. When an earlier removal could not complete because another subsystem still held a reference (the TCP stack takes one on the local address of every connection, in tcp_conn_new() and on connect()), the address is left in place with is_added cleared and is_used still set. A second removal of such an address decremented the reference count again, consuming a reference owned by that other holder. When it was the last one, the address slot was released, its NET_EVENT_IPV*_ADDR_DEL event fired, and the slot became reusable while the holder still believed it owned a reference.

Every address lookup helper matches on is_used and not on is_added, so a half-removed address stays visible to the rest of the stack and repeat removals are readily reachable from remote input. Under IPv6 SLAAC, an on-link node that sends a Router Advertisement with a short valid lifetime causes the address to expire into the deferred state; a refreshing Router Advertisement is handled by net_if_ipv6_addr_update_lifetime(), which re-arms the lifetime timer without restoring the reference, so the next expiry performs the second, reference-stealing removal. With CONFIG_NET_IPV4_ACD and DHCPv4, repeated spoofed ARP conflicts for the device's lease drive dhcpv4_acd_event_handler() into calling net_if_ipv4_addr_rm() more than once on the same address. Where CONFIG_USERSPACE is enabled, the net_if_ipv4_addr_rm_by_index() and net_if_ipv6_addr_rm_by_index() system calls let an unprivileged user-mode thread trigger the same kernel-side release deterministically.

The impact is loss of a configured IP address while connections are still using it, and a corrupted reference count that propagates: the slot can be handed to a newly added address, and when the stale holder later tears down, net_if_addr_unref() resolves the address by value and drops the new incarnation's only reference, removing a live address a second time. The affected objects are static array slots and the counter is never decremented below zero, so there is no memory corruption or information disclosure; the consequence is denial of service against the device's network connectivity, repeatable at the attacker's pace.

The fix resolves the address before touching the reference count and returns false without calling net_if_addr_unref() when the address is already marked as removed, so the public removal API can no longer consume a reference it does not own.

items.summary:
The IPv6 Neighbor Discovery code in subsys/net/ip/ipv6_nbr.c flushes a neighbour's queued packets at the end of handle_ra_input(). The Source Link-Layer Address Option (SLLAO) is optional in a Router Advertisement; when it is absent, handle_ra_input() still obtains (or creates) a neighbour cache entry for the RA source via net_ipv6_nbr_add() with a NULL link-layer address, so the entry stays in NET_IPV6_NBR_STATE_INCOMPLETE with nbr->idx == NET_NBR_LLADDR_UNKNOWN. The pending-packet drain loop was entered unconditionally for that unresolved entry.

Each net_send_data() in the drain loop runs synchronously into net_ipv6_prepare_for_send(), which finds the neighbour still unresolved and hands the packet to net_ipv6_send_ns(), which puts it straight back onto the same pending_queue. The loop therefore never sees an empty queue. With a single queued packet it transmits a fresh Neighbor Solicitation on every iteration; with two or more queued packets it rotates the queue with no allocation and no transmission at all. The loop runs in the network RX thread with the global IPv6 neighbour mutex held.

An unauthenticated attacker on the same link can trigger this deterministically: advertise itself as a router, induce the victim to queue off-link traffic toward that router (for example by sending echo requests with an off-link source address) while leaving the solicitation unanswered, then send a second Router Advertisement without an SLLAO option. Spoofing an SLLAO-less RA from the legitimate router's link-local address has the same effect whenever traffic is queued for it. Router Advertisements are processed with no authentication whenever CONFIG_NET_IPV6_ND is enabled, which is the default for IPv6-capable builds.

The result is a permanent denial of service: the RX thread spins forever holding the neighbour lock, so all IPv6 transmission and every other user of the neighbour cache blocks, and the Neighbor Advertisement that would resolve the entry can no longer be processed. The ipv6_ns_reply_timer work item that would normally drop the pending packets also blocks on the same mutex. In the single-packet variant the loop additionally floods the link with Neighbor Solicitations. The fix restricts the flush to resolved entries (nbr->idx != NET_NBR_LLADDR_UNKNOWN), leaving the packets queued for the NS reply timeout. There is no memory-safety impact.

items.summary:
Flowintel disabled TLS certificate verification for all MISP API connections and used unverified SSL contexts for IMAP and SMTP STARTTLS mail connections. This allowed an on-path (man-in-the-middle) attacker positioned between Flowintel and its MISP or mail servers to impersonate the remote server and intercept sensitive data.

Affected connections include:
- All MISP HTTPS API calls (event retrieval, attribute search, event creation, connectivity checks, and API validation)
- SMTP STARTTLS connections used for sending email notifications
- IMAP TLS connections used for fetching mail archives and testing connectivity

An attacker who can observe or intercept network traffic between Flowintel and the MISP or mail server could:
- Capture MISP API keys and mail credentials (SMTP/IMAP passwords)
- Read all threat intelligence data exchanged (events, attributes, objects, reports)
- Inject or modify threat intelligence data returned to Flowintel

The vulnerability required no authentication on the part of the attacker and no user interaction; it was exploitable by any party with a network position between Flowintel and its configured MISP or mail endpoints.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

items.summary:
Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix_live_view allows an authenticated user to mount a router-mounted LiveView without the on_mount hooks of its live_session via a phx_join message that carries neither a "url" nor a "redirect" key.

The catch-all clause of the private Phoenix.LiveView.Channel.authorize_session/3 in lib/phoenix_live_view/channel.ex accepts a join without a URL for any session, including a root LiveView mounted at the router. The channel then mounts the LiveView with no route, and only a route adds the live_session hooks to the mount lifecycle. Checks that those hooks perform on the connected mount do not run, and event checks that they attach through attach_hook/4 are never attached. The attacker needs a valid session token for the LiveView, which only the HTTP render issues, after the hooks pass there. on_mount hooks declared in the LiveView module still run.

This issue affects phoenix_live_view: from 0.16.0 before 1.0.20, from 1.1.0-rc.0 before 1.1.34, and from 1.2.0-rc.0 before 1.2.14.

items.summary:
On November 20, 2026, we released versions 19.6.1, 19.5.8, 19.4.10 for GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. These versions contain important bug and security fixes, and we strongly recommend that all self-managed GitLab installations be upgraded to
one of these versions immediately.
GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated are already running a patched version. GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action.
GitLab Dedicated was previously protected through internal-only releases 19.5.7 and 19.4.9, which contained interim mitigations for these vulnerabilities; all fixes from those releases are also included in 19.5.8 and 19.4.10. GitLab releases fixes for vulnerabilities in patch releases. There are two types of patch releases:
scheduled releases and ad-hoc critical patches for high-severity vulnerabilities. Scheduled releases are released twice a month on the second and fourth Wednesdays.
For more information, please visit our releases handbook and security FAQ .
You can see all of GitLab release blog posts here . We are committed to ensuring that all aspects of GitLab that are exposed to customers or that host customer data are held to
the highest security standards. To maintain good security hygiene, it is highly recommended that all customers
upgrade to the latest patch release for their supported version. You can read more best practices in securing your GitLab instance in our blog post. Recommended Action We strongly recommend that all installations running a version affected by the issues described below are upgraded to the latest version as soon as possible . When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected. Important guidance for self-compiled GitLab installations: The fix for CVE-2026-132825 is a patch to Ruby. Official GitLab Linux packages and container images already include the patched Ruby. For self-compiled installations, you must rebuild the Ruby installation used to run GitLab with Ruby 3.3.14 or 3.4.13 (or a later release in the same minor series), which include the fixes for CVE-2026-132825 and the other vulnerabilities disclosed in the Ruby security advisory , as described in Ruby . Security fixes Table of security fixes Title Severity CVE-2026-132825 (vulnerability in ruby ) Critical The severity shown reflects the Critical rating assigned by the Ruby security team in GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 . MITRE rates CVE-2026-132825 as High (CVSS 7.4). As this is a vulnerability in Ruby rather than in GitLab’s own code, the severity is taken from the upstream advisory. CVE-2026-132825 (vulnerability in ruby ) This release addresses the security issue CVE-2026-132825 ( GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 ), a heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings in ruby , by updating the version of Ruby bundled with GitLab. This issue has been remediated on GitLab.com, and in GitLab CE/EE versions 19.4.10, 19.5.8, and 19.6.1. In GitLab, under certain conditions, changing the case of a crafted string can result in an out-of-bounds heap write. The Ruby security team has stated that this flaw may allow remote code execution in some scenarios. These versions also include fixes for all of the other vulnerabilities disclosed in the Ruby security advisory Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String . Impacted Versions: GitLab CE/EE: all versions before 19.4.10, 19.5 before 19.5.8, and 19.6 before 19.6.1 Bug fixes 19.6.1 [19.6] Restore Ruby 3.3.12 regexp patches [19.6] Bump Ruby to 3.3.14 Backport 19.6 release notes to 19-6-stable-ee [19.6] Bump GITLAB_CNG_MIRROR_REF to restore Ruby 3.3.12 patches [19.6] Bump Ruby to 3.3.14 and 3.4.13 19.5.8 [19.5] Restore Ruby 3.3.12 regexp patches Backport of ‘Bump webauthn gem to 3.4.4’ Backport of ‘Count Geo secondary registries in a single pass’ [19.5] Bump GITLAB_CNG_MIRROR_REF to restore Ruby 3.3.12 patches Backport: Publish the Pulp repository if the uploaded RPM is not published (19-5) B

items.summary: Security event analysis in large enterprises can be overwhelming, as each alert typically requires manual in- spection by human operators. This process is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies, especially in high-volume Secu- rity Operations Center (SOC) environments. In this work- in-progress paper, we present RAVEN: Retrieval-Augmented Vulnerability & Event aNalysis, an agentic framework designed to support SOC analysts by automating the initial stages of alert investigation. The proposed system leverages a Self- Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based approach to provide an initial classification of security events and enables interactive refinement through analyst-in-the-loop queries. Un- like traditional approaches that rely on generic mitigation strategies, RAVEN generates context-aware remediation sug- gestions by incorporating knowledge of the target enterprise infrastructure. We implement an early-stage prototype and report preliminary results on three balanced test sets of 400 curated web payloads each (SQLi, XSS, SSTI) and a qualitative case study of mitigation generation; an evaluation on IDS- generated alerts and a user study are ongoing and outlined as remaining work.
items.title: RAVEN: A Self-RAG Based Agent for Threat Classification and Response

items.summary: AZOWL AgentOps provides shared governance for deploying agents and delegating work to them. Human and agent senders can exchange messages or explicitly delegate a business task. Accepted work has a stable identifier that links the sender's authority, the assigned runner, any required approval, and result evidence. The default enrolled customer PC profile is read-only. We compare AZOWL components with a configured LangGraph application in 28 synthetic runs across four paired pilots. Original AZOWL services checked work admission, recipient routing, and workflow prerequisites in isolated tests. The configured LangGraph application supplied business task and dispatch records in application code. Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and issued zero writes when an approved delivery address changed. AZOWL's scope gate, exercised as a component, requested approval again on the same task. A product probe reused one registered provider across two workflows and checked prerequisite enforcement for ticket-task submission. The paired protected writes, including ticket creation, used mock providers. Of two deployed PC inventory reads with verified receipts, we traced the 0.6.57 run from submission through runner pickup and tool execution to the receipt, with matching local and central artifact hashes. A separate deployed GRC audit followed an operator-driven ticket lifecycle on sample records.

items.summary: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.
items.title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning

items.summary: The standard 5G Authentication and Key Agreement protocol (5G-AKA) authenticates subscriber credentials but does not verify the integrity of user equipment (UE). Existing literature includes admission-time device-certificate authentication and Trusted Platform Module (TPM)-based measured-boot attestation, which can additionally verify that the UE presents enrolled device credentials and boots into an approved state. However, these checks do not reveal whether harmful unauthorized software is executed after admission. We present TRACE-5G, which continuously verifies the UE's runtime software state and uses the resulting trust state to control network access. TRACE-5G retains the pre-admission certificate and boot checks, and in addition places the admitted UE in restricted connectivity while runtime integrity is verified. Linux Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) records runtime software measurements, TPM PCR (Platform Configuration Register) cryptographically accumulates them, and Keylime, a remote-attestation framework, repeatedly evaluates TPM and IMA evidence against enrolled references. A Trusted result grants full access on the existing PDU session, but an Untrusted result withholds or removes full access and causes network deregistration. We implement TRACE-5G on an srsRAN/Open5GS testbed with a hardware TPM2.0 UE and core-side firewall enforcement. Across ten trusted trials, Level 2 access was established in 9--12s. Across ten untrusted trials, promotion was consistently withheld; in a representative trace, restrictive policy was applied within 5ms of the Untrusted decision and UE-context release completed within 1.670s. TRACE-5G extends UE trust beyond admission without any modification of the standardized 5G protocols.
items.title: TRACE-5G: Trust-Aware Runtime Attestation and Continuous Enforcement for 5G User Equipment

items.summary: Security protocol analysis has emphasized message-passing, as this is how different principals interact in authentication, key exchange, and similar functionalities. However, in many protocols a principal also maintains mutable state that limits what actions its local sessions may take; this cross-session state is altered by other local sessions. In this paper we show how to represent this cross-session mutable state in the strand space approach to symbolic protocol analysis, and how to implement the resulting ideas in the Cryptographic Protocol Shapes Analyzer CPSA. The key theory is expressed in two axioms characterizing state, plus protocol-specific rules. It leads to tight, specific characterizations of protocol behavior in relevant cases, and aids in developing correct protocols relying on cross-session mutable state.
items.title: Mutable State in Enrich-by-Need Security Protocol Analysis

items.summary: AI-driven attacks learn the models of cyber-physical systems (CPS) by passively observing controller and plant signals, then use this knowledge to act covertly. Because covertness depends on the accuracy of the identified model, degrading that accuracy is a viable countermeasure. This work applies Adversarial Machine Learning as a defense, injecting small perturbations into the measurements the attacker observes to degrade an artificial neural network (ANN)-based system identification (SI) attack. The perturbations are derived from input gradients of several independently trained identification models, aggregated into a generalized perturbation, and confined to the transient regimes that carry most of the dynamic information. A sparsity parameter further restricts them to the most influential samples, with negligible cost in effectiveness. On a simulated DC motor networked control system, the proposed perturbations induce larger prediction errors than stochastic poisoning of equal root-mean-square magnitude, and the advantage widens as the magnitude grows. This limits the defense's operating range, which is intended for decoy environments such as CPS honeynets. Additional results indicate that the designed poisoning signals can also degrade N4SID-based system identification, providing evidence of their transferability beyond the ANN-based models originally targeted.
items.title: Gradient-Based Defensive Poisoning Against System Identification Attacks on Cyber-Physical Systems

items.summary: Local differential privacy (LDP) is vulnerable to output manipulation by malicious clients. Zero-knowledge proofs can enforce correct report computation, but clients may still selectively drop out after inspecting their outputs. Prior work combines zero-knowledge proofs with homomorphic encryption to hide reports from clients and prevent selective dropout, but incurs substantial computational cost. We instead develop a three-message lightweight verification framework for robust histogram estimation that uses proofs of plaintext evaluation to restrict output manipulation to selective dropout. Across the evaluated settings for PI-RAPPOR and Hadamard Response, mean per-client online latency remains below 500 milliseconds. We further establish tight error bounds showing that, for RAPPOR, PI-RAPPOR, and Hadamard Response, restricting malicious clients to selective dropout reduces attack-dependent error by a factor proportional to the square root of the domain size compared with output manipulation. Additionally, when client protocols cannot be modified, we propose server-side consistency checks for RAPPOR and Hadamard Response. These checks improve robustness without client-side cryptography and can be applied post-hoc to collected reports, offering an alternative under different deployment constraints. Experiments demonstrate that both verification and consistency checks substantially reduce attack error for certain mechanisms, with consistency checks yielding errors intermediate between those obtained with verification and those under unrestricted output manipulation.
items.title: Robust, Lightweight Locally Differentially Private Histogram Estimation and the Role of Dropout Attacks

items.summary: State machine replication protocols are usually proven secure in the honest-Byzantine setting, which requires an honest supermajority of validators. Deployed systems offer no such guarantee: validators participate for profit and may deviate from the protocol whenever doing so increases their gains. In our work, every validator is rational or Byzantine, and none is honest. Rational validators may collude with each other and with the Byzantine ones, who may also bribe them to deviate. Known impossibility results show that, without honest validators, clients that decide whether to accept a transaction based on a non-interactive certificate and without further communication cannot be kept safe. To bypass these results, we let clients relay the certificates they receive to full nodes and wait before confirming transactions. We also assume that one full node, whose identity is unknown, is honest and always online. Under this assumption, we build a finalization layer over any certifiable quorum-based protocol in a synchronous network. Clients run an existing freezing gadget and fetch past certificates from the honest full node, which makes the protocol \emph{always-safe}: no two honest clients confirm conflicting ledgers, for any strategy of the validators. We incentivize participation through rewards, which the adversary may use to bribe rational validators into censoring transactions. In this setting, we formalize censorship and characterize it tightly: paying only with his rewards, the adversary censors less than a $\bw$ fraction of the available fees at each height, where $\bw$ is the fraction of the quorum he signs, and every coin of censorship beyond that comes from his own funds.
items.title: Playing the SMR Game with Existential Honesty

Consequently, class-level statistics used by existing detectors may flag benign feature deviations while overlooking poisoned samples that blend into the class distribution. In this paper, we propose Semantic Counterfactual Residualization (SCR), which uses a small set of clean reference samples to account for benign variation through sample-specific feature reconstruction. SCR identifies poisoned samples by detecting coherent deviations from these clean baselines, without requiring prior knowledge of the attacks. We evaluate SCR through experiments covering twelve dirty-label and clean-label attacks across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. With a small clean-reference set, SCR achieves attack-averaged true positive rates above 99.5\% and false positive rates below 2\% on each dataset, outperforming eight representative detection baselines in macro-TPR.
items.title: SCR: Detecting Backdoor-Poisoned Samples through Clean-Reference Residuals

items.summary: Forensic investigators must decide which suspicious files to examine first. Machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) malware detectors usually return a bare score that neither explains why a file deserves attention nor signals when changing data make the model unreliable. We present a framework for Windows Portable Executable (PE) malware forensic triage that works only on pre-extracted static features and never executes malware. A calibrated maliciousness score sets each file's triage priority, and a per-sample feature attribution explains the prediction. A per-sample consistency score measures whether the top attributed features agree with documented behaviors from the Malware Behavior Catalog (MBC) and MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques & Common Knowledge (ATT&CK), where the available features support such interpretation. Conformal evaluation and statistical distribution tests flag drift. Each file receives one investigator-oriented triage output. The evaluation protocol, specified before testing, uses a time-ordered split of EMBER2024 as the primary dataset and BODMAS for family disjoint checks, and compares every component with simple baselines on predictive performance, prioritization effectiveness, explanation quality and robustness over time.
items.title: Drift-Aware Explainable Prioritization for Windows PE Malware Forensic Triage with Semantic Consistency Checks

items.summary: Keyword Private Information Retrieval (Keyword PIR) allows users to retrieve data associated with specific keywords from a database while protecting query privacy. However, existing Keyword PIR schemes supporting boolean retrieval either incur high computational overhead due to multiple database traversals, or fail to support universal boolean computation. We propose PMKPIR, a novel keyword PIR scheme supporting both parallel multi-keyword queries and universal boolean computation. We utilize the single instruction multiple data (SIMD) capability of BFV homomorphic encryption to propose an interleaved batching method, and design IBPIR based on this method, achieving the private matching of multiple keywords in a single database traversal. Furthermore, we design a boolean query processing method, extending the parallel capability of interleaved batching from keyword querying to boolean query computation, to support universal boolean computation and accelerate boolean operations. Building upon IBPIR, we integrate this method to further design PMKPIR. To the best of our knowledge, PMKPIR is the first Keyword PIR scheme to support multi-keyword batch matching within boolean queries. Security analysis demonstrates that, consistent with existing PIR schemes supporting boolean retrieval, PMKPIR preserves the core security guarantees of classic PIR. Compared with state-of-the-art schemes, PMKPIR reduces query time, communication overhead, storage overhead, and peak memory by up to 79.06%, 75.00%, 97.92%, and 80.26%, respectively.
items.title: PMKPIR: Parallel Multi-Keyword PIR with Interleaved Batching for Private Boolean Retrieval

items.summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) now underpin the visual encoders of most multimodal models, but this success comes at a cost: relying on third-party pretrained checkpoints leaves these systems open to backdoor attacks. Existing test-time detection methods rely on either the predicted label or intermediate embeddings, limiting their applicability across diverse tasks and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we study how backdoor triggers affect the multi-head attention mechanism of ViTs and identify two distinct anomalous patterns: $\textit{complete attention hijacking}$, causing the attention to exhibit abnormally high inter-head spatial overlap, and $\textit{partial attention hijacking}$, causing an abnormally large variance in the concentration of the attention distribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose $\textbf{DetectViT}$, a test-time backdoor detection method that requires neither training data, model outputs, nor any prior knowledge of the trigger. DetectViT quantifies the two hijacking phenomena via an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score, with thresholds estimated from a small out-of-distribution (OOD) calibration set drawn from an arbitrary source. Across four representative attacks, diverse architectures (DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA), and downstream tasks (image classification and captioning), DetectViT substantially outperforms all baselines with as few as 64--128 OOD calibration samples, achieving a true positive rate of $100\%$ and a false positive rate of $0.17\%$ on BadCLIP. Notably, it introduces negligible additional overhead by relying solely on attention weights already computed during inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/siquanhuang/DetectViT.
items.title: DetectViT: Test-time Backdoor Detection for Vision Transformers via Inter-Head Attention Discrepancy

items.summary: Superspecial curves of genus two over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$, and the rational $(2,2)$-isogenies between their Jacobians, are the vertices and edges of the graph on which genus-two isogeny-based cryptography is built. Let $C$ be such a curve, with Jacobian $J$ and Frobenius endomorphism $π$. We show that $π^2 = p\,α_*$ for a unique automorphism $α$ of $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ whose action on the Weierstrass points is the square of that of Frobenius. For $p \ge 7$ this gives the list of Frobenius types of the Weierstrass points: eight types, each with its Weil polynomial, a congruence condition on $p$, and its number 15, 3, 3, 7, 1, 1, 3 or 1 of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational $(2,2)$-kernels; when all Weierstrass points are rational, the 2-Tate pairing on $J[2]$ is determined by $p \bmod 8$. We then prove closed formulas, in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders and of $ζ_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt p)}(-1)$, for the mass of the curves of each type and for the mass of the rational kernels whose quotient is a product of elliptic curves. For $π^2 = \pm p$ the total masses are due to Ibukiyama and to Xue and Yu; our proofs use the 2-adic Tate modules, the symmetry of the Richelot correspondence and Eichler's mass formula, and, for the other curves, modules over orders of a quartic CM field. The kernels are counted through gluings of supersingular elliptic curves. As a consequence, the proportion of rational kernels with decomposed quotient is of order $p^{-1/2}(1+L(1,χ))$, where $χ$ is the quadratic character of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})$. All formulas agree with an exact enumeration for the 37 primes $7 \le p \le 173$. Finally we describe the graph of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational Richelot isogenies, which is far from connected in the range computed, and discuss what these results say about its use in isogeny-based cryptography.

items.summary: Web applications compose the core of internet services, rendering them prominent targets for audacious attackers. Among web attacks, SQL injection (SQLi) remains a persistent, damaging web applications connected to databases. The widespread adoption of HTTPS has been a critical advancement for online security, ensuring the confidentiality and integrity of communications by encrypting network payloads. However, it also renders traditional Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) less effective, as these typically rely on packet inspection of plaintext traffic. To access encrypted payloads, some NIDS resort to TLS-interception proxies, which leads to data leaks and security risks. This paper presents FlowSH, a system for detecting web attacks that is agnostic to whether the traffic is encrypted (HTTPS) or not (HTTP). Rather than decrypting packets in transit, FlowSH correlates flow-level metadata (NetFlows) with endpoint logs, which inherently contain decrypted payloads after reaching the web server. The system combines unsupervised machine learning to flag anomalous NetFlows and similarity search over server-side logs using Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to confirm attacks. We implemented and evaluated FlowSH in a testbed with multiple web scanners and demonstrated its detection effectiveness, detecting 70% of SQLi attacks missed by ModSecurity, a leading web application firewall.
items.title: FlowSH: Detecting Web Attacks by Correlating Anomalous Network Flows and Endpoint Logs

The TLS option generated for an Ingress carrying the nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-secret annotation was named after the Ingress namespace and name. As a result, two Ingress objects sharing the same host, the same client CA secret, and the same client-authentication mode produced two distinct TLS option names for that host. Traefik treats this as a TLS options conflict and falls back to the entry point's default TLS configuration, which does not request a client certificate, so a route configured with nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-tls-verify-client: "on" becomes reachable without a client certificate. items.summary:
Commit `23e8cca3136a` hardened the search-result title against insert-tag/XSS by setting `$objTemplate->title = StringUtil::specialchars(StringUtil::stripInsertTags($arrResult[$i]['title']))`. But the legacy HTML5 template does not use that `title` variable - it prints the raw `link` variable, which is assigned without escaping.

## Impact

Affected configuration (important): on 5.7.9 the default search template is the Twig `search_default.html.twig`, which does not use the raw `link` variable and auto-escapes - so a default Twig install is not affected. The vulnerable raw echo is in the legacy `search_default.html5` template (still shipped and selectable in 5.7.9, line 8: `<?= $this->link ?>`); exploitation requires that legacy template to be active for the search module (common on sites migrated from earlier Contao / using custom template selection). Where the legacy template is used, the sink is unambiguously raw and `ModuleSearch::compile()` assigns `link` from the entity-decoded indexed title.

A backend page editor can store script that executes for anonymous front-end visitors (and admins) viewing search results, a stored XSS crossing the editor -> anonymous-visitor boundary.

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

items.summary:
Channel access is enforced only by the DataContainer voters (`NewsletterChannelAccessVoter` / `NewsletterRecipientsAccessVoter`, requiring USER_CAN_EDIT_CHANNEL), whose `supportsType()` fires exclusively for Create/Read/Update/DeleteAction subjects dispatched inside DC_Table's create/edit/delete methods. The newsletter custom key-actions are dispatched directly by `Backend::getBackendModule()` (Backend.php:324-327) after only the module-level `USER_CAN_ACCESS_MODULE` check; the DC_Table constructor runs no per-record ReadAction vote for a key-action. `Newsletter.php` contains no `isGranted` / `denyAccess` / `isAdmin` / `hasAccess` calls, and none of the newsletter DCAs have a `checkPermission` onload callback.

## Impact

A channel-scoped newsletter editor can inject recipients into, mass-mail, and in some versions, delete/denylist recipients of channels they are not authorized to edit - defeating the per-channel permission model (integrity + abuse of the mail-sending capability).

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

items.summary:
### Summary

Extracting an attacker-supplied 7z archive can write files outside the destination directory. The 7z header stores each entry's path as a UTF-16 name with nothing constraining it to a relative, in-tree path. The extractor joins that name onto the destination and writes to the result without normalizing it or checking that it stays under the destination root, so an entry named `../../etc/cron.d/x` or an absolute path escapes the target.

### Details

In `src/util/decompress.rs`, `decompress_impl` computes the per-entry destination directly (line 140):

```rust
let dest_path = dest.join(entry.name());
extract_fn(entry, reader, &dest_path)
```

`default_entry_extract_fn` (line 154) then acts on that path:

```rust
let file = File::create(path)
    .map_err(|e| Error::file_open(e, path.to_string_lossy().to_string()))?;
```

There is no normalization, no `dest_path.starts_with(dest)` check, and no symlink-entry handling. `Path::join` discards the base when the joined component is absolute, and `..` components are not collapsed against the base. The convenience entry points (`decompress`, `decompress_file`, `decompress_with_password`, `decompress_file_with_password`) all route through `decompress_impl` with `default_entry_extract_fn`, so the default API is affected.

The trust boundary is the archive bytes. Any caller that extracts an untrusted `.7z` reaches the sink.

### PoC

1. Build a `.7z` whose `FilesInfo` contains an entry named `../../../../tmp/pwned` (or, on Windows, an absolute path such as `C:\Windows\Temp\pwned`).
2. Call `sevenz_rust2::decompress_file("evil.7z", "./out")`.
3. The file is created at the traversed location outside `./out`. Targeting a startup/cron path or a config file turns the write into code execution or persistence.

### Impact

Arbitrary file write outside the intended directory (CWE-22 / CWE-23, the Zip-Slip class). On extraction of an attacker-controlled archive, an entry overwrites files outside the destination — config, cron, autostart, or build artifacts — which can escalate to code execution. Reachable by upload-handling backends, malware-analysis sandboxes, mod/game installers, and CI steps that unpack user-supplied 7z files.

### Suggested remediation

Reject any entry whose name contains a `ParentDir`, `RootDir`, or `Prefix` component, or canonicalize the joined path and verify `starts_with(dest)` before creating it. Apply the guard inside `default_entry_extract_fn` (and `decompress_impl`) so the hardening is the default rather than left to each caller. Reject or explicitly opt-in symlink entries.

## Maintainer response

This issue was patched with ef760b61f3535ac8b93006212aef41bfebc237eb and released as `v0.21.1` to crates.io

Consumers that extract attacker-supplied archives received over a network without user interaction should re-score as AV:N/UI:N (≈8.6).

**Fixed in 0.10.0** (PR #12566, commit 7cfc74e47ffab452663be6842d788a5164d9688b): recursive relabel resolution is anchored to the traversal dirfd.

items.summary:
### Summary
storyblok-backup writes files using unsanitized names for Storyblok components, which are content type or schema definitions. This allows a component name containing path traversal sequences to cause backup files to be written outside the intended backup directory. Anyone with component management access in the source Storyblok space, not server access, can plant a malicious component name that causes arbitrary file writes on the machine of anyone who later runs a backup against that space.

### Details
The writeJson function, which takes a folder, a file name, and content, builds the output file path by directly concatenating the backup directory, the folder, and the file name as strings, with no path sanitization or containment check.

For the components resource type specifically, the file name used is the component's own name field, which is free text and editable by anyone with component management access in the Storyblok CMS.

Other resource types are not affected by this same issue. Stories and datasources use their numeric IDs as filenames, and assets have their filename derived by splitting on the slash character and taking the last segment, which strips path separators. This issue is scoped specifically to components.

Since the component name is stored in Storyblok and only read back later when the backup tool runs, this is a stored, second order vulnerability. The malicious value is planted once, then triggers on every subsequent backup run performed by anyone using this tool against that Storyblok space.

### PoC

**Step 1 — plant the malicious component name via Storyblok's Management API:**

curl -X POST "https://mapi.storyblok.com/v1/spaces/<SPACE_ID>/components/" \
  -H "Authorization: <MANAGEMENT_API_TOKEN>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "component": {
      "name": "../../../../tmp/evil-storyblok-backup",
      "schema": {}
    }
  }'

Any Storyblok user with component-management permission in the space (not server access to wherever backups run) can do this through the Storyblok UI just as easily, by naming a new component with this value in the component name field.

**Step 2 — run storyblok-backup against this space, exactly as a normal user would:**

npx storyblok-backup \
  --space <SPACE_ID> \
  --token <MANAGEMENT_API_TOKEN> \
  --path ./backup \
  --types "components"

**Step 3 — observe the actual file write location:**

With the malicious component name above, the tool's writeJson() function builds the output path as:

  backupDir + "/components" + "/../../../../tmp/evil-storyblok-backup" + ".json"

which resolves outside ./backup entirely. Confirm with:

  ls -la /tmp/evil-storyblok-backup.json

The file exists there, outside the --path ./backup directory that was configured, containing the full JSON definition of the malicious component.

**Step 4 — for comparison, confirm assets and stories are NOT affected:**

The same defaultFetch() pattern is used for stories and datasources (fileField: numeric id) and for assets (fileField derived via 
.split('/').at(-1), which strips any path separators from the value before it reaches writeJson()). Only the components resource type passes a raw, unsanitized user-editable string directly into the file path.

### Impact
Anyone with the ability to create or rename a component in the source Storyblok space, which is a content management privilege and not server access, can cause the backup tool, when run by someone else, to write files outside the intended backup directory on whatever machine runs the backup. Depending on the path chosen and the permissions of the process running the backup, this could overwrite existing files at attacker chosen locations on the host filesystem.

Suggested fix: sanitize the component name before using it as a filename, for example by applying the same last-path-segment treatment already used for assets, or by resolving the final path and verifying it stays within the intended backup director

items.summary:
Flowintel , contained a session management vulnerability in its browser authentication mechanism. The session identifier used a bare numeric user ID rather than a credential-bound token, resulting in several related weaknesses:

- Remembered logins (remember-me cookies) remained valid after a user changed their password, allowing an attacker holding a previously issued cookie to retain access indefinitely.
- Server-side session identifiers were not rotated upon login (local, SSO, or remembered), enabling session fixation.
- Self-service email and password changes did not require verification of the current password, permitting an attacker with an active session to modify account credentials without knowledge of the existing password.
- Administrator-initiated password resets did not revoke other browser sessions, invalidate remembered logins, or rotate the affected user's API key.

An attacker who obtained a valid session or remember-me cookie (e.g., through XSS, network interception, or cookie theft) could maintain unauthorized access even after the legitimate user changed their password. Additionally, an attacker with any valid session could change the account's email address or password without knowing the current credentials, effectively taking over the account.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

items.summary: Contrast (Edgeless Systems) before 1.21.0 performs unanchored suffix matching when selecting per-registry configuration in the imagepuller. Config.registryFor strips a single trailing dot and then uses strings.HasSuffix(hostname, fqdn) without requiring a DNS label boundary, so a registry entry such as [registries."ghcr.io."] is also applied to any host whose name merely ends in that byte sequence, including attacker-registered domains such as evilghcr.io. When an image or layer is pulled from such a sibling domain, the imagepuller sends the configured Authorization header (basic auth, registry token, or identity token), trusts the configured custom CA bundle, follows the configured mirror, and honours insecure-skip-verify (disabling TLS verification) for that host. Image integrity is not affected, as image bytes remain pinned by digest in the policy and are validated after the pull. items.summary: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.
items.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research

items.summary: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.
items.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
